units: the writer addresses an acquaintance who had left a device with him
he pulls the older device out of storage and looks it over
he has just bought a recent model of the same kind
the older device weighs twice what the recent one weighs
its metal shell warms up while it is being used
the screen of the recent model renders colors better
the older device opens up so its battery can be replaced
the recent model is glued together and will not open
the writer asks his correspondent for a reply
text: Do you remember that old tablet you left with me before you moved out? I dug it out of the closet last night and set it down next to the one I just bought. The gap between the two made me laugh. The old one weighs twice as much, the thick metal shell warms up the second you open two windows, and the charger is the size of a brick. The newer one slips into a coat pocket, charges while you forget about it, and shows colors the older screen never managed. Still, I will say one honest thing for the old one: it can be fixed. I have already unscrewed the back to swap the battery, while the newer one is glued together and cracks if you try to pry it open. One wins on lightness, the other on being willing. Guess which one stays on my desk? Write back and tell me what you think before you get home.

units: excess heat is what wears laptops down most
built-up dust clogs the ventilation openings
the blockage keeps the fan from cooling the machine
the device throttles its own performance to protect itself
a steady or crackling sound announces the fault
the keyboard turns warm to the touch
the computer slows down for no visible reason
power has to be cut before the case is opened
replacing the fan costs little and takes one visit
text: What wears a laptop down fastest? Heat, says the repair shop that takes us in. And where does the heat come from? From dust, which mats the vents, jams the fan, and forces the machine to throttle itself. What warns you before it quits? Three signs keep coming back. Sound first: a steady rush of air, then a crackle once the fan starts rubbing against its housing. Then the keyboard itself, gone warm under your fingers. And then the slowdown, settling in for no reason you can see. So what do you do? Unplug the machine, back the screws out of the bottom plate, blow the dust outward, close it up. And if the noise stays? The fan has to go, a cheap swap the shop handles in a single visit. Should you open it yourself? The technician hesitates for a moment, then says a careful hand beats a smothered machine.

units: a repairwoman announces that she has found the fault
the person in charge of the place questions her about her diagnosis
a blinking colored light pointed her in the right direction
she cleaned a corroded deposit off the board
she soldered back a wire that had come loose
she warns that the machine must be kept away from the wall
otherwise hot air builds up behind the device
the person in charge promises to move it the next day
the device comes back on once it is reassembled and plugged in
text: The technician set her bag on the bench and said she had the fault. The manager asked what she had found. She told him that an orange light was already blinking when she opened the case, and that it had put her on the trail. Then she explained how she had pulled the board, scraped a greenish crust off one track, and soldered a dangling wire back in place. The manager wanted a guarantee. She answered that the joint would hold as long as the shop stopped pressing the machine flat against the wall, since otherwise the hot air would sit behind it. He promised to move it the next morning. She closed the cover, drove the four screws back in the order she had laid them out, and plugged the thing in while he watched. The screen lit up a pale blue. The manager smiled and said he would never have guessed one loose wire could cost a week.

units: early calculating machines ran on toothed wheels
every added wheel raised the mechanical resistance
that resistance bent the transmission shafts
the number of columns therefore stayed limited
manufacturers set out to do away with moving parts
the electromechanical relay avoided gears but wore out
it also made a sharp noise with every calculation
the vacuum tube was fast but gave off a great deal of heat
that thermal limit led to the solid-state component
text: Before electricity, adding by machine meant toothed wheels linked by pawls. Every wheel added friction; friction called for a firmer push on the crank; and the push ended up bending the shafts. That set the ceiling for such machines: past ten columns or so, the gearing seized. Builders therefore went looking for a way to get rid of the moving part. The electromechanical relay offered a first way out, since it switched with no gears at all, but its contacts wore down and its clack gave away every operation. The vacuum tube came next. It ran faster and quieter, and so hot that each cabinet needed a blower of its own and a steady supply of glass to replace what burned through. That heat, as much as the bill, pushed the workshops toward the solid-state part: cold, tiny, and with nothing inside that moves.

units: a battery that runs down early is not necessarily worn out
three habits account for the quick drain
a display held at full brightness draws the most power
software reaches the network without being used
heat permanently reduces the capacity of the cell
lowering the brightness and setting it to adjust itself is advised
updating for unused software has to be turned off
leaving the device on the charger all night damages the battery
these steps put off the battery swap without restoring it
text: A battery that runs flat before evening worries its owner, though wear rarely explains it. Three habits account for most of the loss. The first is a screen held at full brightness, when the panel draws more power than the processor does. The second is the long list of programs that reach out to the network in the background. The third is heat, since a warm cell gives up capacity for good. The answer comes in three moves. Lower the brightness first, and let the device adjust it on its own. Next, shut off updating for the programs you almost never open. Last, keep the thing out of direct sun, and unplug it rather than leaving it on the charger all night, because a charge pinned at the top tires the cell. None of this brings a battery back to what it was, but it puts off the day you replace it.

units: two employees of one department each receive an unmanned flying machine
these machines are used to examine the roofs of buildings
one of the models is heavy and can be repaired on the spot
the other model is compact and easy to carry
any breakage of the compact model means sending it back to the maker
a gust of wind comes up during the first outing
the compact machine drifts off and strikes a water gutter
one of its blades snaps
its user waits two weeks for the spare part
the two machines are now used according to how exposed the site is
text: Two coworkers in one maintenance crew were handed flying machines the same week, both meant for inspecting roofs. The first picked a sturdy model on a thick fiber frame, the kind whose rotors you swap by hand in seconds. The second went for a light one that folds into a jacket pocket, quicker to get airborne, but where a single broken part means shipping the whole thing back to the maker. The wind came up during their first inspection. The heavy machine held its place over the rafters while the light one drifted and clipped a gutter. A blade snapped clean off. Its owner waited two weeks for a part his coworker carried in the trunk of his car. Since then the heavy one goes out to open sites and the light one to sheltered yards, and neither of them argues about which is better.

units: the power has to be cut before anything is handled
this precaution is presented as one that cannot be undone
a working surface has to be laid out beforehand
the tools include a fine screwdriver and flat pliers
a container serves to hold the screws
the corner screws come out before the edge ones
the screws are of different lengths and their places must be noted
a conductive ribbon ties the cover to the board
a dark charging light indicts the connector more often than the battery
text: Kill the power and pull the charger before you touch anything: that is the one step you cannot take back. Then set up your corner of the table. You want a fine screwdriver, flat pliers, a dry rag, and a small dish for the screws, or they roll onto the floor and you end up crawling after them. Start on the back of the case: take the corners out first, then the edges, and note where each screw came from, because they are not all the same length. Lift the cover slowly, never with a jerk, since a soft ribbon usually still ties it to the board. Now find the charging light: if it stays dark, the trouble is far more often the connector than the battery. Clean it, put it back together, drive the screws in without forcing them, plug it in, and watch the screen before you pack up.

units: a sound fault in a station is reported before sunrise
the departure display then went dark altogether
maintenance workers reach the equipment room shortly afterward
a backup power unit had gone into protection
its red light stayed on without blinking
a stalled fan had heated the cabinet past its limit
the workers replaced the fan and cleaned the filters
the display was brought back gradually, platform by platform
management now requires the cabinets to be checked every quarter
some travelers missed a train change for want of information
text: The call reached the control desk just before dawn: a crackle in the loudspeakers of a station, then the departure board going dark all at once. A maintenance crew got down to the equipment room half an hour later. They found first that a backup power unit had tripped into protection, its red light steady rather than blinking. By midday the cause was plain. A stalled fan had let the cabinet climb past the temperature at which it shuts itself down. The crew swapped the fan, cleared the filters, and brought the supply back in the early afternoon. The board came alive platform by platform, in the reverse order it had died. That evening management announced that the cabinets would be checked every three months instead of once a year. No train ran late, but travelers missed connections with nothing to tell them.

units: an adjustable lamp is aimed at the working surface
printed boards are stacked up waiting to be repaired
a pencil mark shows the burned area on each board
the soldering tool sits in its holder and is still giving off smoke
the smell of resin has soaked into the walls of the room
the craftsman has practiced this trade since the shop opened
runs of melted metal have marked the floor
the seat has left four pale round marks
having no window forces air to be drawn out at all times
the noise stopping signals a break in the power supply
text: Over the repairman's bench, a jointed lamp leans down toward an orderly mess. Green boards wait their turn in a stack, each one marked with a pencil stroke where the circuit went black. On the right the iron rests in its holder, its fine tip still smoking with the smell of resin. That smell has soaked into the walls, because the man has been soldering here since the shop first opened. The floor keeps a record of the trade as well: drops of solder melted into the covering, and four pale rings worn in by the stool. Since the room has no window, an extractor fan turns above the door without stopping, and its steady drone ends up passing for silence. When it cuts out, he lifts his head sharply, because that hole in the sound means the power has gone and a joint has just been ruined.

units: putting something back in order often costs more than buying it new
the writer blames this imbalance on how products are designed
a battery held on with adhesive makes taking it apart harder
screws with an unusual head call for tools kept for them alone
a soldered link instead of a plugged one draws the job out
makers justify these choices by keeping water out
a compressed gasket and ordinary screws would hold just as well
the writer proposes that board schematics be published
he asks that parts be sold at what the components cost
the obstacle is commercial and not technical
text: Fixing a thing ought to cost less than replacing it, and it seldom does. The fault lies not in the labor but in the design. A battery glued to the frame, screws with heads that nothing standard will turn, a ribbon soldered where a plug would do: each of those choices adds half an hour to the job and turns a cell swap into a full teardown. The defense offered is keeping water out, yet a compressed gasket and ordinary screws hold it out just as well for almost nothing. Three measures would be enough: require common fasteners, publish the board schematics, and sell spare parts at what the components cost. None of them calls for a technical breakthrough; all of them run into a trade that lives on replacement. As long as a sealed device costs less to build than one that opens, the bench will keep unscrewing sealed shells.
